speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our sense is that we should leave the composition and makeup of the council to individual MCSTs and the SPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Any MCST council is made up of owners who wish to volunteer their time to make their estate a better place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Every SP who steps forward wishes to contribute in some way or other.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If SPs are concerned about how representative their council is of the SPs in their estate, then they should be prepared to step forward, serve and be counted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsiang suggested setting a more stringent requirement for the "half-hour rule" which allows general meetings to commence if there is no quorum by the appointed meeting time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we appreciate the intention behind this suggestion, there is a practical issue, of course, to consider.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The problem is that some MCSTs experience poor attendance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Raising the bar for the application of "half-hour" rule may pose practical difficulties for these MCSTs to proceed with their general meetings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This may be detrimental if there are critical decisions relating to safety or maintenance that need to be made.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also mindful that any adjournment of the meetings will incur additional costs for the MCSTs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, it is open, of course, to MCSTs at the general meetings to decide, and members to decide, whether they wish to carry on after invoking this rule or to postpone it to another day, where more SPs can attend.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsiang also suggested putting on hold all decisions made at general meetings where the 30% quorum was not met.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SPs would then have a 30-day period to challenge these decisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The concern is that such a move might be counter-productive as it will open many decisions to review and essentially lengthen the process of decision-making.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All SPs have a stake in the management and maintenance of their developments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we hope that they make the effort to attend general meetings or at least appoint a proxy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This also addresses the query by Mr Melvin Yong on why AGMs can be allowed to commence without a quorum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong sought clarification on what constitutes "safety" in the context of "safety equipment" which SPs can install without the MCSTs' approval.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will depend on the purpose of the equipment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, grilles, when installed at a balcony, will be deemed safety equipment as they serve the purpose of preventing fall from heights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Er Dr Lee asked for the definition of "safety equipment" to be extended to cover other items.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked if SPs, particularly the elderly and handicapped, could be empowered to seek assistance from Government agencies directly for matters relating to safety, security, hygiene and barrier-free access.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are already existing regulatory requirements on matters concerning building safety, environmental health and barrier-free accessibility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For such issues, MCSTs can always approach the relevant Government agencies for their assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If SPs and MCSTs still cannot see eye to eye, the Bill has set out procedures for the resolution of certain disputes, such as by going to STB.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked about the definition of "common property" which is being amended by this Bill, and his concern about the possibility of engendering further disputes between MCs as well as SPs on what amounts to "common property" and whether they can proceed with their own renovations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I would agree, lawyer to lawyer, that the more definitions you put in has never dissuaded lawyers from helping to create more disputes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But always, we rely on the good sense of SPs and MCSTs to determine and dissolve the disputes amongst themselves and to resort to dispute resolution, including alternative resolutions, or to go to STB if these things stand in the way of a resolution.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if MND had plans to help subsidise lift installations in old private apartments without lifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Melvin Yong and Miss Cheryl Chan asked for dispute resolution platforms to address disputes through mediation, rather than legal action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Specifically, Mr Gan asked if we could set up a mediation centre with industry experts and legal professionals to look into claims and disputes between new home owners and developers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are happy to say that existing mediation platforms, such as the Singapore Mediation Centre and the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS) Conciliation Panel, are already able to provide this service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Melvin Yong suggested having a mediation board to resolve common disputes in MCSTs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For that, we have the STB to hear and resolve a list of MCST disputes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The list includes disputes on costs of repairs and rectifying a complaint in respect of a defect in a lot or common property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Alternatively, SPs may approach the Community Mediation Centre (CMC) when the disputes are between neighbours or with neighbouring developments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If mediation fails, SPs may seek legal advice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked about the available recourse if there are disputes hampering efforts to replace or repair common facilities for safety reasons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, for safety critical situations involving structural defects in the building or common property, or any health hazard to the development, or if a Notice or Order has been served by any public authority on the MCST to undertake certain works, then the MCST must comply.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It has powers under the Act to carry out the required works.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked about the situation where MCSTs take action against SPs in a situation where modifications had been made by previous SPs which were unauthorised changes made to their lots.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the contract for the Sale and Purchase between the SPs follows the terms in the conditions of sales from the Law Society of Singapore, then the new SP has the recourse of referring to adjudication under the Fourth Schedule of the Conveyancing and Law of Property Conveyancing rules of 2011.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because the previous SP, who is a vendor to the contract, had undertaken that he has not carried out any unauthorised additions or alterations to the property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, it depends on the form of contract.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of course, MCSTs may initiate action against the former SP under common law, if it wishes to do so, for any breach of duty and care in relation to duties set out under section 37(3) and 37(4) of the Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Building defects are a common subject of disputes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked if the DLP could be extended until 12 months after the first AGM.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will help home buyers make more informed choices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It will also put some pressure on developers and contractors to ensure that they deliver good quality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef spoke on the issue of water leakage and asked if there could be guidelines to advise SPs on handling such issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the case of inter-floor leakage, the premise is that the floor finishing and/or the underlayment above the floor slab has been damaged, which then leads to water seeping through the slab and into the lot below.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While the slab is deemed as common property, its definition explicitly excludes any layer that is the floor finishing or underlayment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Taken together, the leakage is deemed to originate from the strata lot above.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, it is the responsibility of the owner of the lot above to either prove otherwise or repair the defect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in the case of lateral seepage, the party responsible for repairing the defect would depend on whether the leak originates from the interior of a strata lot or from common property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, if rainwater seeps in through an external building wall which is common property, the MCST will be responsible for any necessary repairs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For good neighbourliness, the relevant parties should first explore an amicable solution by cooperating to investigate and repair the leak.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Parties could appoint a Building Surveyor to assist with the determination of the source and cause of the leak.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Alternatively, parties may seek recourse through mediation channels like STB and CMC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The proposed amendments to the Act were meant to balance between the necessary regulatory oversight to safeguard the interests of SPs, and an architecture that is flexible and gives latitude to make self-governance possible for MCSTs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These amendments are the result of many rounds of consultation over the last few years and we hope that the proposed amendments will help SPs as they step up and get involved in their respective councils and estates.
